subsubtopic: SUGGESTION INSTALLATION OF AUTOMATIC ELEVATORS IN CONFEDERATION BUILDING BE DELAYED PENDING REPORT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. During a time when the government is preaching restraint and austerity, it has come to my attention that the Department of Public Works proposes to spend $875,000 for new automatic elevators in the Confederation building on Parliament Hill.
In light of current economic conditions and the need to spend in more relevant areas, such as medical research, coupled with the fact that the fate of the elevator operators is uncertain, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That this House instructs the Speaker of the House of Commons, the Minister of Public Works and the President of the Treasury Board to put a halt to any installation of automatic elevators in the Confederation building until they prepare a report for this House determining the following, whether such an expenditure is necessary at this time, what savings will result, and what duties will be assigned to present elevator operators; furthermore, that no commitment be made to have operators on the automatic elevators.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the President of the Privy Council both in that capacity and in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister. I should like to ask him a question with respect to the announced intention of the government to establish a national lottery scheme. Could the minister confirm for me that it is in fact the intention of the government to seek parliamentary ratification for this major undertaking through nothing more than a routine supplementary estimate, an estimate which will not even be debated in this House and which, like all this government's spending, will

fall under the so-called guillotine for automatic approval before the end of June?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LOTO-CANADA METHOD BY WHICH PARLIAMENT WILL RATIFY PROPOSAL-DURATION OF SCHEME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House leaders and I had some discussion of this matter the other day. It will be recalled that when the President of the Privy Council announced the intention of the government, there was some discussion as to whether it would be possible to dispose of a bill within a reasonable time. It was quite clear from the comments which were made at the time that there was a difference of view amongst the parties as to the wisdom of proceeding in this way. The Leader of the Opposition supported the idea in principle; the NDP opposed it. Therefore, it seemed to me that it would be impossible to get agreement on the kind of procedures which would be necessary to get this bill through within two or three days, which was mentioned during that exchange of views.
I also sounded' out the parties on the possibility of getting an agreement amongst the parties on a time limitation under Standing Order 75A, which obviously was not agreed to. I therefore put before the House leaders the possibility of dealing with this matter through a supplementary estimate. Of course, this supplementary estimate would be referred to a standing committee where it could be discussed in detail. Members of the opposition could, if they wished, bring that supplementary estimate before the committee of the whole on an opposition day and cross examine the minister in whatever way they wanted. For example, we are prepared to have a day when the appropriation bill is before the House to have a full debate, so I do not think in any way the procedure which seems to be preferable would interfere with an adequate discussion in the House.

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the hour of adjournment interrupted my remarks a few days ago I advanced to the House the proposition that I did not consider the question before us at this time as a question of whether we should or should not abolish capital punishment but, rather, a question of whether we should or should not reintroduce some form of capital punishment in our country.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has said on many occasions outside this chamber and inside that he will not sign an execution order. In fact, in response to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who spoke on the opening night of this debate and who expressed his views about the necessity to retain some form of capital punishment in our country, the Solicitor General screamed across the chamber: "If you want to hang someone, get yourself another boy". In opening my remarks I advanced the proposition that the people of Canada do not have an opportunity to get themselves another "boy" until the government dissolves this parliament, calls another election and carries on a dialogue with the people about that. For that reason, the question of whether we should retain capital punishment is irrelevant until the year 1978, 1979 or whenever the government decides to dissolve parliament and consult the people as to its performance.
Now that I have put the question in the proper perspective, I should like to deal with the main points used by the Solicitor General to demonstrate to the so-called "misguided" 80 per cent to 90 per cent majority of Canadians why they are wrong and the government knows better. First, he articulated a strong case on the element of error involved in the judicial process. During the debate on Bill C-83 the same minister demonstrated the reasons for stricter gun laws by rolling out statistics on criminal acts in which people fell victim to gun-toting murderers. Five people daily are butchered with guns, and while not all victims are law-abiding citizens, they are nevertheless murdered. These figures increase drastically if one takes into account other forms of capital crime which do not include guns but which are murder in the first degree and also punishable by death.
Since the abolition of the death penalty for capital crimes in 1963-because that is when it was abolished; no one has been executed since-only 18 persons have been convicted of murder punishable by death. Of these, 11 are still on death-row waiting for the angels of mercy and the defenders of human dignity to come to their rescue. If one considers that the courts dealt with 829 persons charged with murder punishable by death since 1961, and that only

568 were convicted, 82 received the death sentence and 18 were condemned of which only two were hanged-before the period 1971 to 1973-the margin of error referred to by the minister is extremely slim, if indeed there is a margin at all.
The minister also quoted statistics to support his argument that juries are reluctant to consider guilty verdicts for fear that their action will result in the death sentence. Juries are made up of responsible Canadians from all walks of life, and I assume that this will always be reflected in their judgment. Of course, there is evidence to that effect. After all, we are only dealing with the premeditated, contract killer who has had access to all the avenues of the judicial process and has not received a recommendation for mercy or leniency from any source. The minister argues that a much greater percentage of convictions is achieved against criminals charged with lesser offences. The reason for that could be, of course, that our courts and our jury system provide for a degree of discretion, charity and compassion, and recommendations are often made to apply a lesser charge.
Next, the minister charged that the judicial process is unfair. It is very noteworthy that he said that only the poor are convicted of murder and the rich buy their way out of,trouble with money and influence. Is that the reason the government is so reluctant to bring matters which have interrupted the normal proceedings of the House for so long now before a judicial inquiry? Should the government not be responsible for correcting that situation, rather than reacting to it? Do the judges in Canada, who are appointed by politicians, really receive telephone calls from influential people in public life, and do some of them respond favourably to suggestions made to them? This is what the Solicitor General is implying, and I see no clause in this bill or in Bill C-83 which would offer a remedy to that situation.
It is alarming to me, to the people I represent and to all Canadians that this form of government patronage still exists, particularly when dealing with the judiciary.
The other day the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) made a statement in Vancouver to which the press throughout the country reacted. One of the major newspapers in my constituency telephoned me and asked for an interview. They wanted a list of the lawyers who represented Central Mortgage and Housing and government agencies in the city of Prince George. I telephoned the managers of these agencies in the city but was told that the list could not be given to me; it was confidential. There really was no problem. I suppose there must be a number of lawyers who support my political cause in the city, but none of them have complained to me. They are kept very busy and they do not get any business from CMHC or IDB.
I told the managers that if the list was secret I had to suspect there was something to hide. I telephoned the minister and he admitted that instructions are given to the managers in the various regions about which legal officers they should use in their business dealings. He was kind enough to send me a list of the solicitors who work exclusively for Central Mortgage and Housing in Prince George. As it happens, one of them was my Liberal opponent in the
May 14, 1976

last election. He is a good and diligent lawyer, so I have no quarrel with that. Four or five of the lawyers on the list are known Liberal fund-raisers and supporters. This is the kind of thing that Canadians object to in 1976, Mr. Speaker, and the kind of thing that has to be corrected if we are ever to have a greater degree of respect for the political process.
The minister says that civilized society which respects, above all, the human dignity and life of every individual cannot allow itself to consider the cost of enforcing our laws and the incarceration of criminals. I, for one, would applaud that argument if the government could demonstrate to me that this civilized attribute of charity applies equally to the criminal and the victim. It costs the taxpayers of this country up to a quarter of a million dollars to bring to account a person who deliberately challenges the institution which is the guardian of our law and standards of moral conduct. It costs up to $20,000 annually to keep a person incarcerated and isolated from the community. I, for one, cannot applaud that argument. Is it not fair to make a comparison between that and what we as a civilized society afford ourselves in the way of social services?
Are we making restitution to the victims of crime? Do we apply the same degree of generosity to our senior citizens, the handicapped, the socially deprived and the children who in our country go to bed hungry every night? Of course not, Mr. Speaker. Our charitable human instincts only surface when people confront the establishment out of sheer frustration and deprivation. The more violent the confrontation, the more understanding we become.
I cannot help but respond to the letters I get from my constituents who compare the contract killer who has killed a young policeman, with his widow, who is living on a meagre welfare income of $260 per month, trying to bring up two children and provide them with the means of competing in society when they grow up. We must consider what it costs to bring a person to justice and keep him incarcerated. This degree of charity is evident even inside our prisons. The murderer and hardened criminal is interviewed by the press and examined by the "head-shrinker". He receives the attention of every do-gooder who has ever dissected a pickled frog and has discovered he can grow whiskers. The prisoner who is a guest of the taxpayer for just a minor offence and strives to build merit points to support his parole application gets hit over the head with a lead pipe in the ballpark and lives in protective custody without colour television and most of the other essentials of modern-day prison life.
Mr. Speaker, many of my colleagues speak about whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent to murderers. I do not think that is the question which should concern us at all. I do not even think that we need to apply the term "punishment". The only thing we need to consider is the right and responsibility to protect ourselves against those who show wanton disregard for our traditional values, and no respect for human life.
The Solicitor General told me on one occasion, privately, that he actually considers capital punishment an incentive to murder. It would take quite a measure of imagination to think that to a conclusion. He reasons that the murderer has no regard for his own life and that is why he confronts the establishment: therefore, he dares the system, by his
Capital Punishment
violent act, to put him out of his misery or, on the other hand, attach some meaning to his existence-a headline and a picture in the paper on the morning of his execution. The conclusion to this argument is, of course, that if society fails him he must continue to try to get our attention with an even more violent act. I cannot help but wonder in how many cases of the murder of prison guards and policemen this may have been the motive.
Mr. Speaker, I advocate the retention of capital punishment because we cannot condone having the ultimate value of living peaceful and fulfilling lives threatened. We have a right to protect ourselves against subversive and dangerous elements not just from outside our borders but also from within. The Solicitor General is right, execution is final-the condemned murderer will never kill again- and this has nothing to do with revenge or punishment. It has to be viewed as the removal of a cancer which cannot be allowed to exist in a healthy system once it has been identified as incurable.
Many of my colleagues have drawn comparisons between ourselves and countries which have already abolished the supreme penalty. None of their arguments hold water. Invariably they are making these comparisons with countries which have evolved social structures much more advanced than our own. For instance, Belgium-a country which has repeatedly been quoted-can trace the beginning of a cultural evolution back 2,000 years. Unlike our country, all people there are indigenous. The Belgians have two official languages, as we have, but their ethnic groups are not separated by a vast geographical expanse and economic disparities.
Mr. Speaker, what is more important is the fact that in Belgium, as in most other countries which have abolished capital punishment, it was done because the people themselves, not their governments only, were ready to have it abolished-and that is good. In most cases, referendums were held and the behavioural attitudes of their citizens were closely monitored. Superficial comparisons are, for that reason, not fair. One has to make an assessment of the attitude of the people and measure the degree of intellectual maturity of a society with which comparisons are made.
We have in our country today still a small percentage of illiteracy. I know this shocks a lot of people, but unfortunately it is true. In Belgium this has not been a problem for 150 years. This can be demonstrated in other areas as well. Why, for instance, is it that Germany has the lowest rate of labour disputes in the world, whereas we have the highest percentage of man-years lost as a result of industrial strikes and disputes? I suggest the reason is the adversary system to which we adhere in this country but which other countries in part have overcome.
Certainly, this fact alone cannot be attributed to the utter incompetence of the present government, even though it is a key factor. It must be viewed in the light of a fundamentally different approach to work and the work ethic, an approach different from that of our own industrial society. Just as our unions and business managers are not sufficiently mature to consider more advanced methods of labour relations, so 80 per cent of Canadians are not prepared to afford themselves the luxury of trading-off an

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
element of protection inherent in the imposition of capital punishment against extended prison terms.
One would think, Mr. Speaker, that our government should direct some of its attention to the need to accelerate the evolutionary process of which I spoke. It is also interesting to speculate to what extent the government should get involved in setting the direction in which our own distinctive culture should evolve. Do we wish to assimilate the "good guy-bad guy, happy-ending" society which dominates our neighbour to the south, or should we espouse deeper, more realistic values of human behaviour? These questions would come into play if we concerned ourselves more with preventing crime in the first place instead of only reacting to the effects of criminal acts.
In my opinion, we should examine closely the effects violence on television has or will have on future generations. We should subject our educational system to close scrutiny. Is our teaching process attuned to the contemporary need of our times, or are we offering our young citizens an utopian dream instead of preparing them for the society of today? Certainly, the post-war period, which brought with it modern teaching techniques, did not produce a society which is more rational in its relationship with the rest of the global community. We have not been able to make fundamental changes to the adversary system which dominates, not just our judicial system and industrial relations process but the political process as well.
Indeed, I feel that having less of the adversary system in this very chamber would be a step in the right direction. I feel that our Fathers of Confederation settled more of their differences in a consultative fashion than we are able to do today. The law reform commission made reference to and recognized this fact in its report tabled in the House just a few days ago. We have, as a nation, not become more charitable, nor are we using a more compassionate approach in our dealings with underdeveloped countries. The reason for this is, in part, that our own country is still underdeveloped, not just in an industrial but in a human sense.
Just as we still arm our military personnel with weapons not only of defence but of aggression, just as we still consider it our right, indeed our duty, to defend our country and the interests of our friends against aggression in a territorial as well as a political sense, and just as we are still prepared to kill the aggressor without an evaluation of the innocence or guilt of the individual whose life we are taking, so do we have the responsibility to protect our society from the fear of death inflicted on it by the criminal elements within our borders. I do not say it is right and proper that this should be an ongoing process, but this is the reality of 1976, the reality of the times.
I have the greatest respect for my colleagues who do not agree with me and whose conviction is not altered by political expediency. I, too, wish the world would be a better place to live in, a place without fear of war, hunger and suffering. But, Mr. Speaker, it is not. I, too, wish medical science and the science of human psychology were advanced to the point where remedial action were possible to deal with sick and criminal minds. But it is not.
My colleague, the hon. member for Yukon, our party's critic of the Solicitor General's department, and a reten-tionist, spoke earlier in the debate about war. He spoke of

his own experience as a bomber pilot over enemy territory discharging death and destruction on innocent people. He spoke of the fear he suffered in valuing his own life, and the deterrent the fear of death was to his making another trip. It is no secret to my colleagues that I, as a young boy, was on the receiving end of what was discharged from the aircraft in which my friend was a passenger. What a crazy world this is! Surely it would have been a source of comfort to me then, at the age of 12 when the war ended, to know that Erik, too, was scared-although I do not believe that he was nearly as scared as I was, because I have much grey hair and he still looks much younger than I do. To understand how Erik and I feel about all that today, one would have had to experience what we went through. But it should not be too difficult to understand why we both feel that if it were only possible to identify individuals who cannot be taught to conform with the norms of human justice, such individuals ought to be dealt with before they learn to operate in groups. God only knows what sort of a world we would have today if someone had had the fortitude to deal with Adolf Hitler before his rise to power.
It is true that society as a whole is partly to blame for its mistakes which often result in the dissidence of some of its members. But no society is truly free unless it is prepared to work diligently to correct its mistakes and prevent them from recurring. I also sympathize with the person who would have to make the final decision and put his signature to the execution order if capital punishment were returned. But surely this has to be one of the burdens he must bear if he competes for his mandate and the trust and confidence of the people who elect him to his office.
Today, Mr. Speaker, 80 per cent of people throughout Canada wish to retain some form of capital punishment. The reason is that they feel insecure and cheated by their political leaders who demand one thing of them and do another thing themselves. Canadians have been told too many untruths. They fear that the government is not really serious in its attempts to tighten the judicial process and restore the principle of law and order. The 25-year mandatory sentence provision could be rescinded next year once capital punishment is abolished. That is how some people feel. After all, this very government, in 1974, fought an election of the issue of wage and price controls. It said that we did not need such controls in the free society in which we live. Once the government was elected, it brought these controls in-and some people think the program will not work. People have lost faith and confidence in the group of individuals who sit opposite. They do not think they are really serious about tightening our bail provisions and doing those things which will restore peace, order, security and trust in our system.
The people have lost confidence. Between 85 per cent and 90 per cent of our people are worried. It worries me, as it does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General, that we should be part of a society of so-called barbarians who want to kill people. I, too, would like to abolish capital punishment. But we cannot, because society is threatened and 85 per cent of the people of Canada have lost faith in the system. For that, the government is partly to blame.
The peace and security package is only a charade, as the "just society" was and as the "free vote" the Prime Minis-
May 14, 1976

ter has promised will be. Most members of the cabinet will not be guided by their conscience or by the direction given to them by their constituents; they will be guided by their political ambitions. Even ambitious Liberal backbenchers will fall in line. There is, however, a provision, and I advance that to my colleagues across the way.

I was saying that Liberal backbenchers will also fall in line when the free vote is taken- the free vote promised for Bill C-84 which is the subject under debate. There might, however, be an incentive for some of them to defeat the bill, if for no other reason than the fact that the Solicitor General would have to resign. Canadians in all parts of our country will learn, from the results of the final vote on Bill C-84, not only the extent to which our system will protect them from violent criminals, but also the extent to which our present government has removed itself from the popular demands and the will of our citizens.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as I can see, today's debate seems to have become some sort of a tradition established by this government. Indeed, I was listening to my colleague, the hon. member for Rober-val (Mr. Gauthier) and many others. They had the opportunity to take part in three debates on capital punishment since they received their mandate as representatives of their constituents.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, it is the first opportunity I have to speak on a bill to abolish the death penalty. Since the last debate dates back to 1973 and I was elected at the 1974 general election, I imagine that all hon. members who were able to speak during all those debates must find it utterly ridiculous to keep harping on the same issue. The Canadian people do not elect and pay their member to see him start considering all over again the same old bill without ever coming to a final solution in keeping with the feelings and the wishes of the majority.
Although I did not take part in the previous debates, because, as I said earlier, I was not the member for Villeneuve, I cannot help finding utterly ridiculous the situation in which we find ourselves today, because of the stubbornness and the obvious lack of goodwill and common sense showed by the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand). One thing is clear: he is consistent. In some people, it may be a quality, but the stubbornness of the Solicitor
Capital Punishment
General of Canada verges on monomania and obsession and he is bent on abolishing capital punishment. Failures do not stop him.
Year after year, election after election, he introduces a bill to abolish the capital punishment. Although he knows full well that most Canadians are against abolition, what does he care. All the members of the House have refused up to now to abolish capital punishment, for it is obvious that the constituents all across Canada will lose faith in their members should they dare go boldly against their wishes. But all that, Mr. Speaker, does not refrain the Solicitor General from coming back once again with yet another bill. It must be recognized that, this time, he was well prepared along with his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). They are beginning to be called the "Laurel and Hardy" of Parliament, Mr. Speaker. They came along with their peace and security package which is a mixture of thousands of all kind of provisions among which we can find, if we look closely, the abolition of capital punishment.
Why is it that the minister did not come openly and directly with a bill advocating abolition of capital punishment? Why did he feel obliged to devise a colossal joke such as the so-called program on public peace and security instead of simply trying to abolish capital punishment outright? In our opinion, it is merely because the minister knows that the great majority of Canadians are in favour of maintaining capital punishment. Consequently, he is using hypocrite methods and diverted means to impose his will to the people.
Mr. Speaker, is that democracy? The minister's position is shocking. He does not care at all about the opinion of Canadians. It seems to us that the minister is so intelligent that he can decide what is good for everyone, without taking into consideration the views of the people. This is the philosophy that prevailed in the days of the cave-man when the law of the mighty was the law of the land. However, with civilization, we have discovered the concept of democracy which means, in our opinion, that the voice of the majority must determine the course to be followed. The minister does not believe in that. Even when the majority of Canadians, even when most Canadians, believe that the death penalty should be imposed, he himself believes that his views must take precedence and that the death penalty should be abolished.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot have confidence in the Solicitor General now in office, because his credibility has shrunk to 20 below zero. Indeed, if you remember, in 1973, he succeeded in having a legislation passed restricting the death penalty to people killing policemen and prison guards.
This same minister, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has not even been able to implement his own 1973 legislation up to this day. He has systematically prevented the law from being applied to people who had murdered policemen and prison guards. Today, Mr. Speaker, the same minister is back again. He stands before us as if nothing had happened and he is asking us to have faith in him and to pass this bill he has introduced. I say to him, Mr. Speaker, that if he wants our confidence, he has to show

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
his mettle first and implement the existing legislation. How can he hope to gain our support when it is a well-known fact that he does not have the guts to implement the laws voted here by the people's representatives?
The Solicitor General announced recently that he would resign, and we cannot even be sure of that. We can no longer believe what he says. Once he asked that we support him on something and then he turned around and did the very opposite. He told us: "We will hang only those who will have murdered policemen or prison guards". And later, this same minister refused to apply the law.
Mr. Speaker, the death penalty issue is much simpler than some would have us believe. As regards our duty as legislators, is is obvious: we must respect the will of the people. The true issue is not to manipulate statistics the way we like. It is well known, and even hon. members opposite know, that figures and statistics can be made to say almost anything.
As far as we are concerned, what must guide us today in this debate is not our personal opinion or that of the Solicitor General but rather that of most Canadians. That is why many times have asked the minister for a referendum and I ask him again today. A referendum should be held on the issue of capital punishment. The government refuses to allow such a referendum in spite of all the representations to that effect from all parts of the country and all groups of citizens. Why do they refuse? Simply because the government has no intention of listening to the majority. I quite agree: there are Liberal members who are willing to listen to the majority of the people they represent, and I congratulate them for it. However, most of them and especially the Solicitor General, know that the vast majority of Canadians want the death penalty reinstated; but they have no intention of respecting the wishes and aspirations of that majority.
The Solicitor General, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of a soldier on parade with his regiment. His mother, standing amidst the crowd, is saying: "Look at my son on parade. Do you see, he is the only one marching in step?" As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General has the same kind of reasoning. The vast majority of Canadians call for reinstating capital punishment, but the Solicitor General, the only one in authority, says: "I am the one who is right. I am abolishing the death penalty though no one agrees with me". Mr. Speaker, as we say back home, a fellow like that is "bull headed".
I have here, Mr. Speaker, letters that came to me from my riding. As the hon. member will notice, there is quite a pile of them, and I have others in my office. Then, Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General of Canada may have an idea what reaction his bill is provoking in my riding. It is too bad, Mr. Speaker, that he is not here in the House now. He may not be as blind as he seems to be deaf. He might see that people from Villeneuve-like all Canadians, for that matter-do not agree at all with his attitude when it comes to capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, if I read all the letters I have received, the Solicitor General would undoubtedly be retired, perhaps he would be drawing his old age security pension by the time I got through reading them.
Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to mention that the Federation of the Chambers of Commerce of Abitibi-Temiscamingue, through its chairman Mike Amadio, sent

me a letter on May 15 last to ask for a referendum on capital punishment. That is why a few days later I came in the House to advocate a referendum on the matter because, in my opinion, the Chamber of Commerce represents a vast majority of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, I can give you another example. I received a letter concerning capital punishment from one of my constituents. Mr. Wellie Rossignol from Louvicourt, who proposes that members of parliament ask the residents of their ridings to express their opinion on capital punishment. He also suggests-and I find it very clever on his part-that only those who call for the abolition of capital punishment pay themselves for the support of murderers. That way, abolitionists will have to bear the full consequences of their vote. It is not logical that those who agree with capital punishment be obliged to pay for the support of gangsters who are kept alive simply because of those who oppose capital punishment. Logically, Mr. Speaker, those who do not agree with capital punishment should take it upon themselves to pay for keeping murderers alive. Here is another example of letters I receive. This is a questionnaire I sent to all voters in my riding to know about their view on capital punishment. I have received thousands of letters in response to those questions. More than 93 per cent of those who answered have decided in favour of retention of capital punishment. Those figures are clear and, in my opinion, my mandate is clear and is to oppose the passing of this bill. Mr. Speaker, some hon. members make confused speeches, like the one made by the Solicitor General a few weeks ago, to explain that the issue is complicated, that the crime problem will not be solved by resorting to capital punishment and that there is no easy solution. In my opinion, they are wrong.
For any member or minister, the issue of capital punishment should not be complicated. We are not sociologists who split hair or play with statistics to make them say what suits us. No. The member of Parliament has only one way to follow, that is the one indicated by people who have elected him to represent them. Otherwise, there is no democracy. Mr. Speaker, there are and there always will be people who think they are more intelligent than others, people who think they alone possess the truth, people who are always right whereas everybody else is always wrong.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, there will always be people who think they are wiser than others, that they are the only ones to be in step, that they are always right while all others are wrong. Mr. Speaker, they should not sit here in Parliament. Here we represent
May 14, 1976

the people who elected us and we give a voice to those people who trusted us.
Our duty is to reflect as faithfully as possible the wishes and the expectations of those who rely on us and this is why, Mr. Speaker, the question of capital punishment is simple for a conscientious member of the House. All there is to do is to consult-as several members did-their constituents and act accordingly. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this is the role of a member of the House. Otherwise, there is no democracy.
We must admit that Parliament allows the Majority of Canadians to have legislation corresponding to their aspirations and wishes. Hon. members who do not agree with their constituents are facing a very simple problem. It is not difficult at all. If in spite of their disagreement with the wishes of their constituents, they are prepared to represent faithfully those clearly expressed wishes, for them, there is no problem either. On the other hand, if the hon. member is unable as a matter of conscience or ideology to act according to the wishes of his constituents, he only has to resign. It is very simple.
Mr. Speaker, I am fed up with those book worms who are trying to alter the basis of the problem by saying that capital punishment retention is a difficult and frightening issue which is not easy to resolve. It might be true as it is not easy to determine from a laboratory or an office by playing with figures if capital punishment can or cannot deter a criminal from committing a sordid crime. For the conscientious member, capital punishment is simple issue. For me, Mr. Speaker, and the people who elected me, the question is the following: Do they want or not the abolition of capital punishment? Sociologists and criminologists can continue to scrutinize statistics and do research to establish if capital punishment really has a deterrent effect.
For us, what is important is not what a sociologist believes or thinks, but what the majority of Canadians think and what they desire and ask. The solicitor general has many friends among sociologists and it is quite normal. He is their best client as he is always commissioning studies on capital punishment, and giving them subsidies of $1,000 here, $1,000 there, no problem. There is an old maxim that says, Mr. Speaker: Tell me who pays you and I'll tell you who you are.
The Solicitor General is the milk cow which feeds those criminologists who do not know what to do with their ten fingers. Do you think that guys like that would take the chance of making the Solicitor General of Canada angry? In my view, Mr. Speaker, these criminologists are not stupid. He is the one who feeds them, who enables them to live and consequently they prepare the reports he wants, reports which supposedly prove beyond any doubt that capital punishment is not a deterrent to crime.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, this is what they say in all these learned studies made at the back of dusty offices, far from reality. Meanwhile, policemen who are in direct contact with criminals are calling for the retention of capital punishment because they believe that criminals would think twice before killing if they know that they forfeit their own lives. Mr. Speaker, like all other hon. members, I received last week a letter from the executive director of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, Mr. Bernard Poirier, in which he says:
Capital Punishment
We remain categorically and unequivocally opposed to the abolition of capital punishment.
This testimony has to be taken into account since it comes from our policemen, from people who are responsible for the protection of citizens against criminal activities. I also received a letter from Mr. Brown, Chairman of the Association of Metro Toronto Policemen. In his letter, he emphasizes that members of parliament must respect the will of people who have elected them as their representatives.
And he indicated that according to a survey by their own association, motte than 87 per cent of Canadians favour capital punishment. These association presidents and police officers therefore urged that capital punishment be retained. So there we have the views of a responsible individual, familiar with criminals because he has met thousands of them. His business is fighting the murderers who endanger the lives of innocent citizens. He has a different knowledge of these criminals than a criminologist such as Ezzat Fattah, beloved child of the Solicitor General. Fattah is typical of the worst, the most dangerous group in social sciences. As I said, he thinks he knows better than the others, than 90 per cent of Canadians. He decided capital punishment is not an adequate deterrent. Police officers familiar with criminals, the people who want to be protected from those criminals, and every retentionist were wrong. He is that kind of a soldier, as I said, who alone walks in step, and so is the Solicitor General. He is the sort of guy who dares say that legislators should not heed the voice of the people.
This is more or less what that fathead stated in his study titled "Canadians and capital punishment", which was financed by the Solicitor General in person, of course. That guy is dangerous because he does not believe in democracy. He thinks the government should listen to him and not be concerned with what Canadians may think. It is with that kind of guys that people wake up in a dictatorship. They believe they are more intelligent and better qualified than every one else to decide what others should do.
In my name, and in the name of all my colleagues, I protest these insulting and ridiculous statements by Fattah the Fantastic who, in an attempt to give more weight to his criminology paper, does not hesitate to suggest people in favour of retaining capital punishment are less educated than abolitionists. But somewhere else, he states there are now more people in favour of capital punishment than 10 years ago.
Then the question arises whether he means that people are now less educated than they were 10 years ago? This of course is utterly ridiculous. People go to school longer. His statistics are based on a bunch of nonsense, just as Mr. Fattah is. People today have easier access to education than before, and this does not prevent them from favouring capital punishment, in spite of what he says.
Anyway, Mr. Speaker, I know people with PhD's as long and as fat as Mr. Fattah, who cannot even tell the difference between a gun and a murderer. They cannot even tell which one of the two is responsible for the murder. The present Solicitor General also belongs to that category of pseudo intellectuals who believe themselves more intelli-

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
gent than 90 per cent of Canadians. Fortunately there happens to be some Liberals who are a little more intelligent than he, as they are for capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, people like that who think they know better are a threat to freedom and democracy. Since we are living in one of the most developed countries on earth, what should matter is liberty and respect for the views of most Canadians. I am sure that Canadian taxpayers would be indignant to hear that their tax money is being squandered by the Solicitor General to pay a fat salary to a guy like Fattah who advocates that the government disregard what the people think. This is the icing on the cake. Not only are we paying taxes, but the money from these taxes is used so that people may tell the government to ignore what Canadians think and want.
This government will not get out of it so easily. The mandate it received in the 1974 elections did not include abolition of capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, I saw the Trudeau Express. I saw the smile of beautiful Margaret, but I never heard the right hon. Prime Minister or one of the government members say during the election campaign that the Liberal party wanted to abolish the death penalty. Yet, the government has now introduced a bill to abolish capital punishment. Despite surveys which show that more than 80 or 90 per cent of Canadians want the death penalty to be maintained, despite the thousands of letters which we receive daily in our offices and in parliamentary offices, to try to make us swallow this bill more easily, the government says that there will be a free vote on the issue.
Mr. Speaker, I want to issue a warning to hon. members who always support blindly their own party. They will have to answer to their voters if they put faithfulness to their party before respect for the wishes of the people they represent or are supposed to represent. As I said earlier, for the members of this House, the issue of the death penalty is not complicated, it is not a moral for a theological or a conscience issue, it is first and foremost a question of respecting one's voters. If the voters, the constituents of a member say that they wish the death penalty to be maintained, the member should vote for the retention of the death penalty. If some members do not understand this, they should not be sitting in this House.
For my part, and I think that this is clear, my fellow citizens of the Villeneuve riding have written to me, and, as I said earlier, I have received thousands of letters from people asking me to oppose firmly the bill introduced by the Solicitor General of Canada, which we are now considering.
If my constituents, as most Canadians, are opposed to the abolition of capital punishment, it is because they are fed up seeing criminals slaughtering with impunity innocent citizens because the law is not severe enough to have a really deterrent effect. Mr. Speaker, these honest citizens, who abide by the laws and who respect their fellow beings, witness horrible and sordid crimes and they know that their children, their spouses could be the next victims of some bloody murder. They also know that, with the death penalty, the murderer can only be a threat to society.
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General himself recognized this fact in his report published in March 1975 when he said that it is just as obvious that the death penalty definitely eliminates the threat that an individual can pose

to society. Canadians are not blind. They can see that criminals are not afraid of the law. If they kill, they are sent to prison for three, four, five or ten years and then they are let free and can go on working havoc. We know that about 300 horrible crimes have been committed in Canada since last year.
I have here an article published in the February 13, 1976 issue of the Ottawa Journal. In this article, it. is said that the 19-year-old murderer who killed a 16-year-old gas station operator during an armed robbery asked the police: "Does it really matter even if I killed him? I am 19 years old, even if I am sentenced to life imprisonment, it won't last more than 20 years because life imprisonment in Canada is imprisonment for a maximum of 20 years. And, if I am lucky, I will be freed on parole much before that".
That is what murderers are saying, Mr. Speaker: Why worry? The worst that can happen to me is life imprisonment. Life imprisonment never means more than 20 years, and often less than 10.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are tired of risking their lives while the same Solicitor General fusses around with philosophy. Canadians want the criminal to put his life on the line. If he takes the life of an innocent, he looses his. Capital punishment opponents often say that life is too valuable for society to execute killers. Those people seem to forget that the lives of the innocent victims are as valuable as those of the assassins. What can we do?
And what can we do to protect and force the killer to put his most valuable asset on the line? That is what justice demands. That is what Canadians demand. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we must take our responsibilities and respect the clearly expressed will of the great majority of our fellow citizens and reinstate capital punishment. When the people have spoken, the government only has to obey. That is the message, Mr. Speaker, I wanted to convey today on behalf of the people of my constituency of Villeneuve.
