subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: There have been two speakers from this party.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Also, one independent member, 14 Liberals and 13 Conservatives. Of those who have spoken so far, about 12 have spoken in favour of the bill, namely, in support of the abolition of capital punishment, and about 22 have spoken against, namely, in support of retaining capital punishment. I know that several members are undecided on this very important matter, and it is for that reason that those of us who have made up our minds feel it is worth while to participate in this debate.
Those who are against the abolition of capital punishment can be divided into two groups, those who have
May 14, 1976

strong personal beliefs, and those who follow the results of a questionnaire that has been circulated in their ridings. In the first group, those who are in favour of retaining capital punishment have so far failed to prove that capital punishment is a deterrent. So far in this debate no one has come up with any evidence to prove that. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the onus is on the retentionists because it is they who propose to take a life in return for a murder. I challenge them to come forward with the proof that the penalty is a deterrent or is an effective preventive measure.
This morning, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) said, if I understood him correctly, that he considers the question of whether or not the death penalty is a deterrent as irrelevant, that it does not mean anything to him, that it is not part of the consideration which we should include in arriving at a conclusion. Instead, he considers illiteracy as a relevant criterion. I reject that argument because it implies that people with better education are less prone to commit murder. I believe it has to be substantiated by facts before this strange thought is put forward for our consideration. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has sent me a correction-for which I thank him-saying that so far two NDP members have spoken in this debate and a third one is to come.
The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River went on to say that he considers it more important to deal with the question of the adversary system in labour relations, that if we had less of the adversary system in this chamber it would be a step in the right direction. I invite the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River to speak to his leader and his frontbenchers to see whether they will heed his advice, but I do not think these considerations are relevant to the question whether in Canada, in 1976, we should continue to have the death penalty on our books.
The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River proceeded by saying that really this is not going to be a free vote, and that it will be a kind of alignment of backbenchers on the government side just to vote for the bill because of our personal political ambitions. I should like to draw to his attention that it has already been demonstrated by interventions on the part of hon. members of his own party that there will be a free vote. Frontbenchers and backbenchers of the Conservative party will be voting for this bill, and therefore they will demonstrate with their vote that this is, and was meant to be a free vote-and quite rightly and understandably so.
Before going on, I should like to be allowed to quote from a book written 200 years ago by a man who was born in the same town in which I was born. In 1764 he published a book about crime and punishment, and this passage translates as follows:
The death penalty cannot be useful, because of the example of barbarity it gives men. If the passions or the necessities of war have taught the shedding of human blood, the laws, moderators of the conduct of men, should not extend the beastly example, which becomes more pernicious since the inflicting of legal death is attended with much study and formality. It seems to me absurd that the laws which are an expression of the public will, which detest and punish homicide, should themselves permit it, and that to deter citizens from murder, they order a public one. Which are the true and most useful laws?
Capital Punishment
That is the question which Cesare Beccaria asked. He was a writer, philosopher and thinker 200 years ago who put what I just read down in a book. He also argued as follows:
The objective of the penal system . .. should be to devise penalties only severe enough to achieve the proper purposes of security and order-
I doubt very much if there are many in this chamber who disagree with this conclusion. He went on to say:
The effectiveness of criminal justice depends largely on the certainty of punishment rather than on its severity. Penalties should be scaled to the importance of the offence.
He continues:
Beccaria was the first modern writer to advocate the complete abolition of capital punishment and may therefore be regarded as a founder of the abolition movements that have persisted in most civilized nations since his day.
Why have so many countries since then done away with the death penalty? If we look at the western world, who is left amongst the countries which apply the death penalty? To the best of my knowledge, in the western world they are France, Spain and some southern states of the United States, because there that is a provincial responsibility.
If the death penalty were the answer, why is the murder rate higher in some countries where the death penalty is practised than in some countries where it has been abolished? The answer to this question must come from the retentionists, from those who want the death penalty, because, as I said before, the onus is on them to prove that it is a measure which does deter. Perhaps the retentionists, following this intervention, might wish to address themselves to this question.
There is another question. Looking over what has happened in the history of humanity, when the death penalty is involved, who is really affected? Is it the rich, the poor or those somewhere in between? We really have not been able to find, in the records of those who have been executed, cases of people who have had the means to pay for a good defence and all possible means at their disposal to protect their lives. However, there is a long list of people who could be considered the weakest elements in society, who could not afford to do so, who were the victims and who were executed because of lack of a sufficient and adequate defence.
I was intrigued by the intervention of an hon. member a couple of days ago when he said that perhaps, instead of carrying out the death penalty by hanging, we should still have the death penalty but we should have it, as he put it, in a gentle manner. It was not elaborated upon, but one could imagine-if we were to have things that way-that perhaps the person to be executed would find a pill served with his breakfast, discreetly covered by a napkin, and a note saying, "Whenever you are ready, please help yourself. We will take care of the funeral expenses, of course". That is the kind of thinking going on in the minds of some hon. members who feel that we should still have the death penalty, but that we should change the way we are to put it into effect.
I know this is a rhetorical question, but what can be done to bring back the lives of those people who are executed in error? Some people say there are not any, or only very few, but even if there were only one it should be sufficient cause for us to pause and think. However, it is

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
more than that. The records of Sing-Sing which have been kept since 1890, prove that 12 per cent of the lives which were taken there were taken in error-12 per cent, or 50 people, who afterwards were discovered to have been innocent. Who is going to bring back those lives, I ask hon. members of this chamber who want to retain capital punishment? Obviously, the answer is no one, because it is too late.
I should like to discuss for a moment the kind of punishment in our society which would stand as the one we would consider to be preferable. Which one is more likely to be remembered; in other words, when life is taken or freedom is taken? Let us consider the following situation in which a life is taken. We have all read about it. It is in the early hours of the morning. It is cold and damp. There is a priest following the man to be executed, saying the last prayers. There is the director of the prison, one reporter, a doctor who has to pronounce the man dead once he has been hanged; there is the executioner waiting there, and next to him there is a strong and heavy person. That is the person who is supposed to throw his weight and hang from the legs of the executed person until they are sure he is dead.
Is that the kind of scene we would like to see happening again in Canada? I ask this question seriously. Surely we do not, and the majority of Canadians do not. If the majority of Canadians were to see a scene like this, they would want to do away with that kind of approach.
What kind of punishment is society more likely to remember and to be impressed by as a measure whereby the state is effective and efficient in catching up with those who have committed a crime? That is the case when freedom is taken away. When a man is kept in an institution for 5, 10, 20 or 30 years of his life, he is daily a physical example, of one who has been taken away. All those who live in that region, who drive by, who read the news, know that he has been taken and continues to receive steady punishment. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) said the other day, these people rot away in the prisons. Other members have said the same thing. This should be a cause of concern to us because such treatment is not human. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is not a reason for supporting the retention of the death penalty in Canada.
The second category that I wish to deal with is all those people who have spoken before me and who are supporters of the death penalty because of questionnaires. When listening to them, I ask myself whether they really believe in making up their minds through means of a questionnaire. It should be remembered that ten years ago Canadian public opinion was in favour of the abolition of the death penalty. Would they have supported that? Suppose that ten years from now Canadian public opinion should swing again in favour of abolition. Where would they stand then? How will they account for the lives taken in the meantime? Will they say, "I go as the wind blows. If it blows from the east, I will vote one way; and if it blows from the west ten years later, I will vote the other way"? Is that the position they will take? I am sure it is not, Mr. Speaker. Are they certain that elected representatives are to be void of ideas on this vital subject? Is that the indication, that they are

empty inside and their opinion is formed as the result of a questionnaire? Is that the thesis they put to this House? I doubt it very much.
We all receive letters in the mail which accuse the cabinet of having acted outside the law when it commutes the death penalty. I think it is important in this debate to put on record that cabinet does not act outside the law when it commutes a death sentence. Section 684(1) of the Criminal Code, approved by this parliament, gives the power to cabinet to commute death sentences. This matter has been raised in many public meetings in Davenport and I have received the question, in the form of letters, from many parts of the country as well.
A debate of this kind would not be complete without some remarks devoted to rehabilitation of inmates in our prisons and the prevention of crime in our communities. It seems to me a system of flexibility and of incentives would permit the rehabilitation of the convicted person. The shortcoming that exists in this bill is that the fixed, rigid terms for murder do not offer any ray of hope, even with the best performance and behaviour. The convicted person will have to wait a fixed number of years for release, regardless of the quality of his conduct in the penitentiary. I would ask for the removal of fixed terms in order that those who deserve it may benefit from the rehabilitation process. I hope that this desirable flexibility will be introduced at committee stage, and if not then, at a time when an atmosphere of better understanding prevails.
I was very impressed when I attended a public meeting in St. Jean, Quebec, organized by a group called ARCAD. This group had held public meetings throughout southern Quebec with the intention of bringing together members of the community and prison inmates with the co-operation of the penitentiary service and the Secretary of State. A lot of tough questions are asked at the meetings, and interesting answers are given in an educational process which raises the perception and understanding of all who participate.
Prevention is a subject that deserves a full debate in itself. From what I know, much needs to be done with the young, particularly those growing up in our large cities. Community workers are necessary in cases where guidance and direction are missing. We should be particularly concerned with the growing number of youngsters placed in the care of foster homes. That is not to say that all foster homes do not offer an adequate environment; most probably do. But there remain a certain number of young people who do not receive adequate attention and grow up according to the rules of the street. Eventually they may drift, picking up bad habits and ending up in deep trouble.
Another question we should ask ourselves in this debate is whether, once a person has been convicted and stored away in one of our maximum security penitentiaries, we can really expect, considering the conditions that prevail in most penitentiaries, that he will again become self-reliant and able to function properly after many years of imprisonment. In view of what seems to be going on in our high-security penitentiaries today, I am sure particularly in places like Laval, that the quality of our penitentiary service needs to be improved.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I offer a challenge to members of this House who really believe in the death penalty

to come forward in this debate with the proof and the facts that will support their thesis that society will be better off, better protected, by its retention. The onus is on the members who are advocating the taking of human life by the state in retaliation for murder; it is on those who want the state to reply to a murder with a coldly calculated kill. If members who believe in the death penalty will not come forward with the facts and the information in support of their stand - and so far they have not - they will have failed to demonstrate the validity and the merits of the stand they are taking in the name of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that Canadians can be better protected by means other than the death penalty- by adequate penalties and punishment for murder, for assault, rape and other forms of violence, with better penitentiary services, by improving the rules governing the release of inmates on full parole, day parole and temporary absence, through crime-prevention measures, through improved social services and with the help of youth workers in the community. Hon. members know that the tendency toward crime starts long before the crime takes place. We have to go to the root of the problem, Mr. Speaker-and the death penalty does not!
The bill before us is a step in the right direction, and I support it.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate today I wish to say that I do not do so with any sense of pleasure or elation. I venture to say this feeling is shared by a great many members, if not all, of those taking part. Rather, it is a sense of responsibility that causes many of us to participate in a debate of such importance. I am sure all of us are aware of the fact that Canadians are alarmed at the breakdown in the administration of justice in this country. They are very anxious for something definite and concrete to be done in order to reverse the trends we now find in society.
A short time ago the House considered Bill C-83, which was designed to reduce the incidence of violent crime. Now we are considering the other bill in the package, Bill C-84, which deals with capital punishment. This is the fourth major debate on capital punishment in which I have participated. As I read the speeches made back in 1966, 1967 and 1973, and compare them with the speeches delivered to date in the debate of 1976, I cannot help but wonder what the government has been trying to prove in consistently bringing this matter before the House.
I made the point in my speech of 1973, which my hon. friend for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) raised as for back as 1967, that the government is using the capital punishment debate as a diversionary tactic to divert public attention from our economic problems. That is one element I wish to bring to the attention of the House, although I am sure many hon. members are perceptive enough to recognize that fact. The second element I wish to bring to the attention of the House is this: regardless of what we in this House decide about this legislation, and particularly if we reject it, the government will still continue on its present course. This government has made up its mind that no one
Capital Punishment
is going to be executed, and regardless of what parliament says it will have its own way.
The government disregarded the will of parliament in 1966 by introducing a new bill on capital punishment in 1967. It has disregarded the will of parliament since that time by automatically commuting the death sentence of every person convicted of capital murder. When parliament, in 1973, extended the partial ban on capital punishment, the government completely disregarded the will of parliament by procrastination and the postponement of justice. In Canada today we have 11 individuals under sentence of cleath.
So I say, again, that this debate is a diversionary tactic. Why else would the government pursue a course which permits 100 speakers or so to participate in debate on the issue? What they say will not influence the direction the government is taking. If this bill passes, I imagine nothing will change. It will make it easier for the government to do what it has been doing in the past. If this bill is defeated, the government will continue to act against the intent of the law as it stands until the economic situation reaches a stage some time in the future where the government will need another diversion. Then, without doubt, we shall have another debate on capital punishment-and it could take place as early as next year if this bill is defeated.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that people are skeptical about the bill. I am skeptical, because it is difficult to be anything but skeptical when we consider the actions and performance of this government. I state that at this moment I am against the abolition of the death penalty and it is my intention to vote against this bill. Nothing I have heard in the three previous debates on this issue or in this debate has made me change my mind. I have listened to all the arguments, including the argument of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), even though he has accused individuals who hold views opposite to his as lacking intelligence, and although he may question our intelligence I can suggest one thing: I know many individuals of the same persuasion as me, but if they were in the position of the Solicitor General and had to implement a law in which they did not believe personally, they would resign. That minister has chosen to ignore the intent of the law, he has talked, in all seriousness about lack of perspective and "stumbling blocks to an intelligent and informed public discussion of the real problem." The latter comment appears on page 13088 of Hansard for May 3, 1976.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Solicitor General himself is lacking in perspective, otherwise he would have resigned long ago because of his views on capital punishment and refusal to carry out the present intent of the law. Furthermore, if the minister wants to talk about stumbling blocks, I say that he and the government are the major stumbling blocks to a reasonable and rational system of justice and administration of justice in this country.
I speak for an area of Canada which has the misfortune to contain possibly as many as 13 penal institutions, including the Matsqui institution in which are housed serious offenders, including a number of those convicted of the crime of murder. I believe that the increase in lawlessness in this country, and particularly the increase in violent crime in my area, dates from the time the former solicitor general stated in the House that from then on the

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
emphasis of the government would be on the rehabilitation of the criminal, rather than the protecting of society. The minister opposite can quote all the statistics he wants, but he, his predecessor and the government must share the blame for the deterioration in the administration of justice in this country.
I have stated on a number of occasions that I am not against the rehabilitation of the criminal. I believe that this rehabilitation is essential. It should be one of our major responsibilities and prime objectives. But I do not believe that it should be done at the expense of the citizens of this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Nobody said that.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I listened intently to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) when he spoke, and I heard his interjection. I suggest that his interjection hardly corresponds with some of the statements which have been made. As I pointed out, the major objective, or the main emphasis, will be the rehabilitation of the criminal rather than the protection of society. If the hon. member challenges my interpretation of the minister's remark, he may look it up for himself.
As we consider the situation in which we find ourselves today, I am sure we shall recognize and acknowledge the fact that rehabilitation is of vital importance. We have been living in a period of permissiveness in society which has shown itself not only in juvenile delinquency but in the lack of ethical conduct on the part of government

I am speaking generally now-which is indicated by charges laid against some in the business community with respect to kickbacks and bribes. It has shown itself in practically every area of our society. You have minor crime and major crime. I believe that this directs our attention to one thing, Mr. Speaker. If we are to solve the problem of crime in Canada, it will have to be done by a redirection of our society. If not, I am afraid the future will be rather bleak, to say the least.
I wish to refer briefly to an article that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, April 10, 1976, headed "Delinquency Casebooks: 'Sick' Facts", written by Journal reporter Ian Haysom. I am sure that all members have read the article so I will not put on the record more than two or three paragraphs. I quote:
A disturbing number of Ottawa teenagers-
We could substitute "Canadian teenagers".
-are dwelling in a world of sex, crime, drugs and violence-and many are encountering deep emotional difficulties as a result, according to social agencies in the city.
Teenage prostitution-sometimes involving girls as young as 13 and 14-is becoming increasingly evident.. . He-
That is referring to a social worker.
-identifies the main problem areas in Ottawa as juvenile prostitution; under-age drinking (and subsequent alcohololism); teenage depression and other psychological problems; promiscuity (leading to. venereal disease and unwanted babies, especially among 14 and 15-year olds); crime (especially vandalism and breaking and entering); the emergence of gangs in certain areas of the town; drug-taking and pushing; and a general trend towards teenage violence.

When we consider this in light of the problems we are facing in Canada, the problems do not just concern the teenagers and juveniles. It is a failure on the part of society down through successive generations, the last several generations in any event, to face up to the responsibility in which justice prevails, honesty and uprightness are characteristics to be desired, and righteousness is exalted above the iniquity we see about us.
While believing very strongly in the principle that in the final analysis we, as individuals, are responsible for our own actions and must suffer the penalty for wrongdoing, I do not hesitate to say that in trading off moral and spiritual values for the seeming benefits of crass materialism and secularism, successive generations are providing the climate in which selfishness, disrespect for the rights of others, and naked violence find ready expression. Spiritual laws have been repudiated, the old-fashioned virtues have been replaced by the so-called new morality, and situation ethics have taken the place of the principle of right and wrong. To the extent that this development has been promoted or countenanced by society, we share in the guilt of those whose activities we are now attempting to curb.
Therefore, one of our main responsibilities is the rehabilitation of those who have been caught up in these trends and circumstances. Instead of elevating and challenging our young people to the highest principles and motivations of life, we have allowed them to drift aimlessly, caught up by these influences that are working for the degredation of human society.
I just give that as background to the main issue before us today. I have pointed out that even though we believe it is important and necessary to retain a system for severe penalties and crime, we must recognize that we have a responsibility wherever we can to salvage, assist, and rehabilitate those caught up in these situations.
I should like to briefly comment on the question of deterrence that the minister likes to talk about so much. He and the government claim categorically that the death penalty is not a deterrent to murder.
I would like to put on the record a couple of quotations from a study of "Punishment: its Severity and Certainty", by Bailey and Smith, published in the "Journal of Criminal Law, Criminology and Police Science", December 1972. I quote from page 531 of this study:
The lesson to be learned from capital punishment is not that punishment does not deter, but that the improper and sloppy use of punishment does not deter or rehabilitate.
This of course makes sense to everyone but the government. The government since 1962 has seen fit to ignore the law and not administer capital punishment, and yet when he wants to quote statistics the minister uses the period since then to back up his claim that capital punishment does not deter. This is the folly of the minister's reasoning.
Severity of the punishment is an important element in deterrence theory, but of equal importance is the certainty of the punishment. It is not enough to have a severe penalty like capital punishment on the statute books. The penalty must be used or it is no longer a penalty.
I quote again from the study:
Deterrence theory suggests that the severity and certainty of punishment are additive factors. That is, when punishments are severe and
May 14, 1976

administered with certainty, maximum deterrence results. Inversely, when punishments are slight and uncertain, deterrence will be minimal. Common sense as well as some evidence, would seem to support these assertions.
Because of time I shall only quote one piece of evidence from a study of crime in the United States in 1968, recorded in the same article:
The average homicide rate of states with low levels of certainty and severity was found to be three times the average for states with high levels of certainty and severity. Eighty-one per cent of the states with both low values of severity and certainty had homicide rates above the nation's average, while only 9 per cent of states high on both severity and certainty had rates above the average.
These facts are very enlightening in view of the many statements the minister and other members of the government have been making on the subject of deterrence. As one last thought on this subject, I would like to point out that we do not hear of many people who would go to the Solicitor General or some police officer and state, "I had intended to kill someone, but I changed my mind when I thought about the punishment."
Several years ago, and this was referred to in some of the previous debates, a man who had been incarcerated for murder and was either on parole or had escaped got into another situation in which the police were involved. When asked why he did not shoot the policeman, he replied that he knew that he could face the death penalty. Regardless of what the minister or anyone else says, there was a deterrent as far as that individual was concerned. We do not know how many others were called upon to make a decision in light of that fact. In reality we do not know how much of a deterrent capital punishment, or any punishment, for that matter, has been. Most people just will not admit, or the occasion will not arise for them to admit, that they have been deterred from committing a crime.
I would recommend the article to which I have referred as good, enlightening reading for the Solicitor General and other members of the government, together with another article published in the journal of the same name in December, 1973, and entitled, "The Impact of Certainty and Severity of Punishment on Levels of Crime in American States: an Extended Analysis," by George Antunes and A. Lee Hunt.
The minister has made much of the so-called provision in this bill which would substitute a mandatory 25-year prison sentence for capital punishment. May I say I do not believe the government has any intention of putting anyone in prison for 25 years. It has no more intention of sending anyone to prison for that length of time than it has of executing anyone should this bill be defeated. I say this because,the bill contains at least one great loophole in this respect-I refer to the provision for review of a sentence after 15 years. If any hon. members remain uncommitted after this debate I hope they will look closely into this aspect.
The bill has been publicized as replacing capital punishment with a mandatory 25-year sentence. I submit that this is misleading. The 25 years is really a maximum sentence; in practice it will more likely be 15 years and perhaps something less than 15 years if the government can find a way to make this possible. This provision can be compared
Capital Punishment
with the measure the government introduced in 1967, and again in 1973, when it wanted the unrestricted abolition of capital punishment. To pacify its own backbenchers it attached to these measures a provision for capital punishment in cases where prison guards or policemen were murdered. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the government had any intention of executing anyone: that provision was attached merely to enable it to get the support of its own members many of whom were opposed to abolition. Similarly, I do not believe the government has any intention of sending anyone to prison for the stated period of 25 years.
I should like to quote from the report of the Law Reform Commission of Canada entitled "Dispositions and Sentences in the Criminal Process." If hon. members have been reading these reports carefully they will understand quite clearly the source from which the government is deriving its ideas. On page 26 we read:
A prison sentence for the purpose of protecting society by separation should not be for more than twenty years.
Elsewhere in the report is an indication that it ought to be a lot less than 20 years, in the opinion of the Commission, so I hope hon. members will not be taken in by this tough talk about 25-year sentences. I would point out that Bill C-83 itself says parole can be considered after 15 years.
In conclusion, may I say that I abhor capital punishment and I abhor murder, but I believe it is necessary for society to maintain the ultimate sanction in order to protect itself. Nevertheless, I am of the opinion that some other method of sanction should be considered in place of the present method. I should like to see a society in which punishment was not necessary, a society in which we did not need jails, and in which people could live in peace. I believe Canada, under the present situation, has gone further away from that goal. It is unfortunate that this should be happening, because until we reach that goal we must live in a society where jails, punishment and, indeed, capital punishment, are necessary facts that face us.
I should like now to refer to two or three letters I have received. I do not intend to read them all, but they were forwarded to me just the other day, together with petitions from my constituents. One of them is directed to me as the member for Fraser Valley East, and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). It states:
We, citizens of Abbotsford District and Matsqui Municipality, located in the central Fraser Valley of British Columbia, are living in the midst of thirteen penal institutions with an inmate population of approximately 2,500 prisoners. Because of the increasing frequency of violent crimes committed by prisoners who have been granted passes and parole, and by persons released on bail awaiting trial, we believe our personal and public safety is seriously threatened by your present system.
Therefore, we petition the Department of Justice:
(1)	to refuse to grant parole or temporary absences to prisoners guilty
of murder, rape or drug trafficking.
(2)	to refuse to grant such persons bail while awaiting trial.
(3)	that these policies be instituted as law throughout Canada and
enforced by the Department of Justice.
The other letter is addressed to myself and to the Solicitor General. It is along the same lines but it has to do with capital punishment. The petition reads:
Therefore, we petition the cabinet and the Attorney General's Department that for all persons convicted of murder the death penalty be maintained and enforced within the shortest time possible.
13540

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
Appended to each of these letters are between 1,500 and
2,000	signatures, indicating the grave concern felt by the people of my own constituency where, as hon. members know, there are some 13 criminal institutions within a small area. Attached to the petitions was a letter from the person who had circulated them. I want to read this letter. Mr. A. B. Patterson, M.P.,
Dear Sir:
Enclosed herewith are two petitions signed by a large number of residents of this area for presentation to yourself and Hon. Ron Bas-ford, Minister of Justice, and Mr. Warren Allmand, on the following matters:
1.	Refuse parole or bail to persons awaiting trial on charges of murder, rape or trafficking.
2.	Maintain death penalty for all persons convicted of murder and penalty enforced in shortest possible time.
On March 22nd, Council unanimously passed the following resolution: MOVED by Alderman (Dr.) K. A. Boulton
SECONDED by Alderman Hougen that we endorse petitions presented for submission to Minister of Justice and Solicitor General. CARRIED:
Yours very truly,

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: I put this on record to show that I am not speaking only from personal conviction when I say I believe we should retain this ultimate sanction so as to make it clear we shall not tolerate cold blooded murder, but that I am speaking on behalf of a great many of my constituents, including those who signed these petitions which are in themselves an indication of the predominance of support for capital punishment which exists across this nation of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose in a way that this long debate on abolition or retention of the death penalty can tempt any of us to a certain amount of cynicism and boredom. After all, the issue has been debated in so many countries, including our own, so many times that we all despair of throwing any new light on such a complex and emotional question.
The one thing of course that all of us agree on, whether we are abolitionist or retentionist in any form, is a respect and reverence for any human life. No matter where we get this from, whether from an innate moral, natural law, child training and or indoctrination or whatever, there is a paradox in this debate in that, although arguments may be heated, each side assumes a reverence for life and a need for protection of society. These are wanted by all.
The abolitionists generally argue that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent to crime and bring supporting arguments from social science studies, including those done by specialists in the field of criminology, as a sub-branch of sociology or social psychology. They likewise point to the evidence of states in the United States that are retentionist, or abolitionist, or countries of western Europe, to show that capital punishment cannot be proven to have any perceptible effect on the murder rate.
The retentionists generally argue on this point that deterrence can be interpreted in various ways; incidentally on this point so can the opinion polls for which some MP's 
seem to have an unwarranted adulation. This is especially true of their own made up private opinion polls which, without the use of proper methodology, can be easily abused. The abuses can be done subconsciously through the way questions are stated, the size and nature of the sampling process, and a whole series of pitfalls that are inherent in the process and known to anyone who has done research and methodology studies is sociology or social psychology. It is even so when trained specialists draw up these questionnaires and polls.
These polls can easily be used on such touchy questions as abolition and abortion for a member to escape from his or her responsibility to put their conscience first. I reject the notion completely that we are delegates here of the people. We are their representatives, and when they put us here they presumably did so deciding that our concern, understanding, and judgment would be brought to bear on these issues, not on what pseudo-scientific opinion polls suggest the majority of Canadians want. They, the people, through the ballot box are ultimately our judges.
The retentionists also argue that the threat of execution has an impact not provided by the threat of very long sentences of even life imprisonment. On the other hand, in 1954 Hugh G. Christie, then of Oakalla prison in Burnaby, B.C., told a special parliamentary committee that executions convinced other prisoners that they were hated, whatever their offences.
The retentionists argue that sometimes murderers are known to have broken out of jail, threatening society all over again. They also argue that the economic cost of maintaining society's most antisocial and threatening members is very high. Why should all Canadians have to maintain such a criminal for the rest of his or her life? The abolitionists reply that the judicial system can make mistakes, that once a person has been executed in error the mistake cannot be corrected. They also maintain that there seems to be a good deal of truth that executions deepen and maintain the violent instincts that are obviously predominant in our culture today, as for example in such popular art forms as movies.
I personally think there is a good deal to this argument, even though I consider its expression by some abolitionists as somewhat one-sided. One of the reasons that I am opposed both to abortions and the death penalty is that I think there is a "fall-out" on people's attitudes which tends, subtly but insidiously, to undermine the special regard we have traditionally held for human life in this country.
I also think that there is a good deal of truth for saying, and a considerable amount of systematic studies among criminologists to show, that juries tend to acquit when conviction means execution, whether by hanging or some other means. The retentionists argue that retribution is part and parcel of human nature and of every society. In fact our whole social and legal system is based on it.
The ultimate form of retribution is execution and social anthropologists have found it used in all societies at one time or another. Some retentionists, as every MP knows form his or her mail, point to its acceptability in the Bible, especially in the Old Testament, and they refer us to Genesis 9, verse 6.
May 14, 1976

Many of the latter are strictly biblical fundamentalists, regardless of what denominations they belong to. They seem either to be unacquainted with, or will not accept, modern Biblical scholarship, and while accepting certain hardcore teachings as fundamental to a Judaeo-Christian concept of life, put much of the scriptures in the cultural context of the times in which they were written. I respect the right of these people to favour the death penalty for premeditated murder. I must say, though, that when some of them use the name of Jesus Christ in support of capital punishment, I see red. If there is anything that all Christians share, and I also include here most Jews as well as Christians, about Christ and his teaching, it is that love, mercy, forgiveness, and compassion are the essence of his life and doctrine.
Granted that we need retribution against murderers for the sake of the safety and cohesiveness of society; that does not argue for the death penalty. I am in favour of the 20 or 25 year imprisonment for premeditated murders, as long as there is judicial review after 15 years and we get some built-in guarantees in the legislation that more of the medical resources of psychiatry, and more and better trained clinical psychologists, are attracted to the prison system by market and other types of incentives.
This decision is a vexing problem for all of us. We have to decide how we will vote in the privacy of our conscience, even if it does not seem to be the popular thing to do now, when pressure groups and opinion polls seem to be trying to persuade us that we should not exercise that precious right but should give in to some vague concept of "collective consciousness" in Canada.
It is obvious to us, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most important duties of government in any society is to protect its citizens against the effects of crime. The only possible reason, as I see it, for a member of parliament to vote for capital punishment would be its proven ability as a protection against murder. I cannot, in my conscience, accept the evidence for this proof as presented by retentionists, and I therefore intend to vote for the abolition of the death penalty in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has seemed to me that since coming to this Chamber your title, Sir, has an ironic twist, for though it is your duty to preserve order in this Chamber it is we who are the speakers, and we whose duty it is to give voice to the region we represent.
Contrary to public opinion it is not rare that we who are parliamentarians have the opportunity to deal with the synthesis of a wide variety of opinions expressed and even unexpressed, together with our own best judgment, but this is called a "free" vote. I submit, Sir, that every vote is a free vote, for every person here is free, due in part at least to the work of succeeding generations of parliamentarians and our democratic process. We are free to reflect in legislation our best judgment in our time, and in my case with a government which understands what liberalism really means in expressing philosophy.
The statute books of this nation at this time retain a law pertaining to capital punishment implemented in 1967, a
Capital Punishment
law which has been de facto abolition. This law states in part that capital punishment is officially and legally suspended except for the murder of a law officer or any prison guard. This law was a product of a time which honestly believed it was on the road to abolition. Like the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) we were all confident that our nation would undergo the basic social changes necessary which would make the death penalty unnecessary.
Then we got a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
If the hon. member has a question, Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to entertain it.
Succeeding governments have commuted these penalties on examination of jury recommendations for mercy or otherwise by Her Majesty's right of clemency. Each time this action was taken by succeeding governments, Mr. Speaker, I submit it was done in the earnest expectation that indeed and at last "just around the corner" a new world, where abolition would be possible, would surely evolve. In my opinion that world, so devoutly desired, has not yet arrived and a decision must now be rendered at last.
The succeeding moratoriums have failed. "All the words have been said"-I quote my dear friend and colleague, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Morin), from the last debate in 1973, and who would be speaking today if she were here. We have basic changes to make in this world of ours and it is to this that our House should address itself before we can consider abolition of the death penalty as a move toward the security of all Canadians.
The most basic areas of change which I foresee as being paramount to a society in which abolition could be adopted are in parenting, child care, education, the media, and penal reform. I will amplify each of these only briefly, since again I am sure hon. members have heard it all before. For instance we blithely assume that, like the animals of nature, human beings are natural parents. Most are not. Parenting is an untaught art in our society, that unique distillation of love and discipline and example which can create in its best evolution a security for children to grow in knowledge of their place and role and responsibility to civilization as a whole.
Child care in our nation is yet another area largely unlearned. The fostering of children, our own or others, can be a richly rewarding service to humanity. But in our world we find neglect and mistreatment of children. We find adult selfishness intervening in the full development of a child's potential. We find children without rights or hope, and without a future.
Today's education seems stubbornly bent, at worst, on reteaching lessons for a world that is past, or in teaching for a world that is only here today and gone tomorrow. Education is an ongoing flow where one is taught not facts but rather the ability and capacity to constantly learn. In an ever-changing kaleidoscopic world of multi-data, all our citizens have a right to know how to think, to organize their lives, and to remain mentally agile enough to accommodate their lives to an increasingly altered and flexible lifestyle. Without such adaptability human beings are under a strain which is intolerable.
95 568-2 314

Capital Punishment
Another needed basic alteration appears self-evident. The media in general, and television in particular, that medium so powerful and all pervading that it can induce a consumer to choose one type of dog food over another, has profoundly changed our lives. But we refuse to come to terms with this fact and with this threat.
I ask members to cast their minds over recent television programs they have observed. Violence, death, and destruction dominate our "entertainment". In one average month on our own CBC there are more numbers viewed in this country than actually occur in the nation in a year. But let us examine those murders more closely. Our home screens portray actors dying quickly, cleanly, and without undue pain. Do hon. members know, let alone young impressionable minds, that television actors must portray violent death without undue anguish, blood, or even without taking too much time in synthetic dying? No wonder our society regards killing as of little lasting importance and believes life is expendable.
Then we look at penal reform. It has been infinitely stated in this debate, and in those that have preceded it, that until this nation is prepared to invest in the rehabilitation process for criminals and violent people in our society we will remain a criminal and violent society. I submit we will be faced, as a result, with taking on the responsibility of deciding the fate of those who so severely transgress our laws as to be non-reformable. Further it must be admitted there are sociopathic personalities who simply cannot distinguish between right and wrong, good and evil and what is acceptable social behaviour. There is no cure for these humans. What is our answer to the problem they represent?
It has been widely stated across our nation that members should vote as their constituents demand. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, contrary to I am sure what most constituents believe, on this particular matter constituents do not speak with one voice but with hundreds and thousands of voices. Parliament is being asked to decide. "Make a decision" is the outstanding theme of almost all who have joined in this national debate. Although an overwhelming majority do indeed desire retention of the death penalty it is true, the variations and gradations of the manner of that retention is a veritable babble of contrasts, and there is no consensus or no clearly defined direction. The option members have, is to follow their own judgment.
I would ask constituents everywhere to consider the words of Edmund Burke who stated, "Your representative owes you not his industry only but his judgment and he betrays you instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion."
In addition to what I consider our social unpreparedness to accept abolition of the death penalty, it is my opinion that it would be both illogical and inconsistent for me to vote for Bill C-84 for the following reasons. I arbitrarily accept that life commences at the moment of conception, a premise which I grant is not universal. In spite of this I endorse our law for therapeutic abortion. This, Mr. Speaker, is the taking of life, and I would refer to my speech in this House on that subject last May 29.
Similarly, although this House has not yet dealt with the ethical-moral problem of the unnatural extension of life by artificial means, and here I must state I consider

euthanasia a misnomer although it must suffice as language is imprecise. This so called "life", artificially extended beyond clinical death over a protracted period of time, is abhorrent to me personally, and I believe not in the best interests of our society. If it were me or someone I loved in such extremity, I pray that the artificial "life" would be humanely terminated.
Feeling as I do on these other matters, it is not in accordance with my philosophy and judgment to deny the retention of our current law which should be duly enforced. Indeed in the case of those who so gravely transgress the laws of our society as to take the lives of those assigned by our society to be our protectors, I endorse the retention of the death penalty within the current law of our nation as one of the admittedly imperfect answers in our search for a secure society.
I submit that we are defining the shape of our national character in this debate and, although some of us might not like what we see, I regret that my idealism does not extend to acceptance of this as the moment in time to acknowledge that we have reached a sufficient level of civilization to allow us to abolish the death penalty, even though I am confident that the day will come when basic changes in our society will make such extreme punishment unnecessary.

Mr. Speaker, although I intend to speak in favour of retaining the death penalty in Canada at this time, I look forward to the day when it will not be necessary in our country. However, the government must accept the responsibility for the rising demand by the .public for retention. Certainty of punishment is the best deterrent to crime we know.
The present laws have just not been enforced in a satisfactory manner-in effect, the government is seen to have shirked its responsibility in this matter. Hon. members have already pointed out that the actual time served in prison by 42 murderers paroled between 1968 and 1974 averaged just over 13 years, and that in 1974 alone over
1,000	temporary absence permits were issued to inmates convicted of capital murder. Surely at this time we would be well advised to retain the death penalty in limited cases of murder rather than to ram this bill through and further diminish respect for the law.
I have the greatest respect for the many constituents who have telephoned and written to me favouring abolition; however, I feel that I represent the apparent majority of my constituents who wish to have the death penalty retained.

I thank the hon. member. I want to preface my question with the

May 14, 1976

remark that I respect whichever position he holds on this contentious issue. I would like to ask him a simple question. Since this is to be a free vote, how can he state in the House, without at least smiling, that anyone is trying to ram the bill through the House?

Mr. Speaker, I do not consider that all of us will be allowed to have a free vote in the House. We will on this side, but I have my doubts about the other side.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) misses the whole point about the trust delegated by the Canadian people to elected representatives. Those who put themselves forward for positions of civic responsibility cannot opt out of that responsibility by claiming it is too heavy for them. We are placed here in Canada to manage our day to day affairs, and short of divine intervention we must uphold our laws.
To say that there is not the slightest guarantee that by executing murderers violence will be decreased, is to beg the question. There may be cases where the knowledge that a murderer, if caught, would forfeit his life, far from having a deterrent effect might have the reverse effect.
Yet there are others-as, for instance, armed men or hunted criminals, not yet guilty of murder, threatening to kill hostages unless their outrageous demands are met. The knowledge that their own lives would be forfeited for certain if they carried out their criminal threat would be far more likely to induce them to avoid committing such a crime. Terrorists are ready enough to risk their lives in taking those of others, so long as they themselves have a sporting chance of surviving. But it takes an exceptional man to act in such a way as to condemn himself to death.
It seems to me that we have to keep the death penalty for certain kinds of crimes. We now have in our federal prisons people who have committed more than one murder, and there is no further punishment that can be meted out. In effect these people have a licence to murder. Take another case of a man who is threatened with life imprisonment for a crime he has already committed. What reason has he not to kill the arresting officer in an attempt to escape? His punishment would be the same. In short, there are many cases where the death penalty is the only penalty available that could possibly deter.
Anyone who takes another's life should know that he thereby forsakes his own and does not just suffer the inconvenience of being put into prison for some time.
Life imprisonment now really means anything, but even if it meant real life imprisonment its deterrent effect would never be as great as that of the death penalty. It is because it is irrevocable that it is the one people fear most, and because it is feared most it is the one most likely to deter. We have all read reviews, such as the one recently printed in the American Economic Review, which state that over the period between 1933 and 1969 an additional execution per year may have resulted, on the average, in seven or eight fewer murders.
If you assume the evidence for the deterrent effect of the death penalty is not clear, you face two risks. The first one is that if you impose the death penalty and it does not have an additional deterrent effect, you have possibly lost the life of a convicted murderer without adding the deterrent and thereby sparing future victims. The second risk is that
Capital Punishment
if you fail to execute the convicted murderer and execution would have an additional deterrent effect, you have failed to spare the lives of a number of future victims. Between these two risks I would much rather execute the convicted murderer than risk the lives of innocent people who could have been saved.
Our system of'punishment is based not just on deterrence but also on what is called justice, namely, that we feel a man who has committed a crime must be punished in proportion to the seriousness of the crime, and since the crime that takes life is irrevocable, so must be the punishment. Once we make it clear to a person that if he deprives someone else of life he will suffer only minor inconvenience, we have cheapened human life, and we are at that point today.
We hear the argument that the death penalty is legalized murder because it inflicts on the criminal the same situation he has inflicted on his victim, yet most punishments are designed to inflict on the criminal what he inflicted on the victim. The difference between the punishment and the crime is that one is a legal measure and the other is not. As for the brutalizing effect, I think that people are more brutalized by their daily TV fare, and probably are more brutalized by our failure to punish brutal acts seriously.
There is no question that there will be a demand for discipline in penal matters. Some of the shocking murders in Canada of late may well make it impossible for the government to hold out against the demand for restoration of capital punishment. I am sure the change in the trend of opinion is there for everyone to see. Even convinced abolitionists are changing their minds, and have come to believe that terrorism is a type of crime for which death cannot be a deterrent available to one side only. There is a strong public reaction present which must precede any general restoration of discipline in our society.
Surely the purpose of criminal justice should be the protection of society, rehabilitation of the offender, and compensation for the victim. Our present system of criminal justice is dominated by the treatment approach, the idea that criminals can be rehabilitated and thus prevented from returning to crime. That is a basic notion of the government, and it is under strong attack.
Our correctional system is not working. Present methods have little effect on the tendency of criminals to return to jail. The basic elements of our probation and parole system were both designed years ago, primarily to handle what we would now really consider mild criminal types. However, we are now dumping serious criminals into this system. We now have a set up operated on the principle that some young fellow with a master's degree in social work can actually treat 75 or more hard bitten convicts over the telephone, or during a half hour interview per month.
No wonder people think it is a farce. What they really do is force convicts to be fakes. Convicts know they must prove to the Parole Board that they are trying to improve themselves if they are to get out. They figure if they have to take a reading course, or physiotherapy, or get up in group counselling, or denounce themselves, or anything else, they will do it. They want out.

May 14, 1976
Capital Punishment
Of course we all know that it is far better to prevent crime than to put people in jail after they have committed a criminal act. Therefore the main thrust of our society should be in the area of crime prevention. We must appreciate that the most effective and essential tool in crime prevention is to reduce people's leaning toward crime, and to develop a stronger national disposition toward observance of the law. This approach must start from the grass roots level. Every institution in our society has a responsibility to bring its influence to bear on this problem, including the home, the church, the school, the media, and all institutions which instil, build, and fortify character and self-discipline.
Without going over all the arguments, perhaps we could look at one reason behind the existence of capital punishment. The historical reason for the death penalty is that in earlier days it was the only way in which the state, that is, our organized society, was able to prevent the perpetual and self-perpetuating orgy of killing. The state took over from the injured individual the avenging of a relative's murder, and imposed the sentence of death itself on the murderer. No longer could the relatives or friends of the murdered man avenge his death by themselves committing murder, but in return for abstaining from doing so the Crown or state assumed the responsibility for seeing that justice was done, and of course the result was that there was a great decrease in the number of private killings.
The abolitionist claims that capital punishment is not a deterrent to would-be murderers. This is an empty argument and completely beside the point. There is no way to determine how many murders were not committed by those who wanted to commit the act but did not through fear of execution.
The question should be, does the supreme crime demand the supreme penalty? In effect, do we place the highest possible value on the life of the victim? There have been some grim pictures brought to mind in this debate about the condemned man going to say his last prayers before execution, and so on. All I can say in reply is that his victim seldom has a chance to say his last prayers.
The abolitionist movement, which has grown so strong in recent years, is not based on any moral grounds, regardless of its claims to the contrary. It is propagated mainly by those who feel that it is somehow the fault of society that men are criminals and that therefore they should not be held fully responsible for their actions. I do not think we should allow capital murder to be passed off as the sin of someone's environment. What I hope to see in our country is people striving to expand the moral factor of our society and relying less and less on excessive regulation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I have complete respect for the opinions on all sides of the House, regardless of which side of the question they support. This is the first time I shall have spoken on this issue, but I have listened very carefully to those who are possibly of a different frame of mind, and I must say that in the first instance I had two speeches prepared because I tried to listen to both sides. Fortunately, I have been able to prepare a third, and since it is almost four o'clock I would appreciate it if I could call it four o'clock and reserve my time so that hon. members

might at least hear my speech in its entirety and so that there can be some continuity.
I would have finished my speech by four o'clock.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I must say that probably this motion should have been seconded by both the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) because while the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (myself) will not be running next time in a constituency quite as large as that which includes the Northwest Arm bridge, the hon. member for Annapolis Valley will probably be running at least at one end of the Shubenacadie River crossing.
I shall begin by dealing with both matters. If I may I will devote ten minutes to each, and hopefully my seatmate, who comes from a part of British Columbia, will remind me with dispatch when I have reached the end of 10 minutes so that I can turn to the other matter.
First I shall refer to the Shubenacadie River crossing. When I first became involved with East Hants which, by the way, started out life in this parliament with representation by the Hon. Joseph Howe, I timidly ventured into its waters and was told that we should not concern ourselves with the perhaps larger issues which were involved with the tidal power which could be developed in the Bay of Fundy. I think we should be concerned-and that is probably the royal "we"-about the crossing between Truro and Windsor on the Shubenacadie River. I fought three elections in my constituency, perhaps not brilliantly but with some success, and I promised the people that I would raise this as a major issue. I have kept that promise, Mr. Speaker.
There has been an earlier debate in this parliament about the possibility of federal participation in providing a crossing on the Shubenacadie River. Such a crossing would complete the transportation link through the south-northwestern part of Nova Scotia connecting the town of Truro with the Annapolis Valley. That was my view when I first represented the area in 1968 and I have not had reason to change my mind.
Even without resort to all the statistics and studies available to us, it seems very obvious to me that East Hants can best be served by a crossing over the Shubenacadie River. It would serve to open up an area that was famous in the days of old wooden ships and iron men, and the whole history of Atlantic Canada. It goes back that far, Mr. Speaker, but it also has very real importance in the present day.
I make no apology for raising the issue again, Mr. Speaker. It has been brought up two or three times in the past eight or nine years, and even then maybe I could have brought it up oftener. I have the satisfaction, however, of having prompted an hour of debate some years back when members from Atlantic Canada raised their voices in support of my motion.
There are several reasons why there should be a crossing over the Shubenacadie River, Mr. Speaker. It is an integral part of the Fundy trail proposed by the Department of Public Works. Many Americans visit this part of our coun-

At the present time they have to start near the port of Saint John, then go through Albert country, through Cumberland County, and by some magic means get to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. Some hon. members may ask why the federal government should be interested in a bridge or a causeway or a tunnel to circumvent the river. Mr. Speaker, the federal government has paid substantial sums of money to make river crossings possible for Montreal and for Vancouver. As you and I know, Mr. Speaker, lots are drawn to determine the allocation of time for private members' business. In that regard I want to apologize to and for the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) who has waited patiently, with a great long speech prepared, to take part in the debate. Yes, who is the hon. member for York North. In any event, I have digressed. One of the classic problems to do with old Halifax was peoples difficulty in getting to work. One could go by way of what we call the Armdale rotary. A short-term solution advanced by many, including the former member representing this area of Halifax who is a colleague of mine, involved specific traffic controls and traffic lights, which can control traffic using the Armdale rotary. off in a different direction altogether; otherwise the city will be paralyzed, and the people mortified.
I wish to propose a solution. I know it is not endorsed by the present administration in Halifax, and not endorsed by the columnist who is the be all and end all when it comes to suggesting things which should be done in Halifax. I will make my proposal now, because I may not be here as the representative of the people of the area another time. I think it would be good if we could spend money to develop Halifax from its end, to the northwest. I think the link should go under, rather than over or on the Northwest Arm of Halifax. It would be tragic to build a great bridge across the Northwest Arm of Halifax, one of the most beautful areas I have seen in the world. It is residential and has no great commercial mix. I realize others can say the same about their own constituencies. I suggest that we could make mistakes, architectural or otherwise, and they should be buried underground.
Let me say this in my final minute or two. About five years ago the Government of Canada was good enough to pledge itself to providing a $25 million fund for what was called the Metropolitan Area Growth Investment Company. I wish to speak on both parts of the motion, Mr. Speaker. From the point of view of regional economic expansion the fact is that the activities of DREE in Nova Scotia, as in all other Atlantic Provinces with the exception of Prince Edward Island, are carried out largely in accordance with a General Development Agreement with the province. The General Development Agreement with Nova Scotia was signed on September 12, 1974. Its purpose is to facilitate joint federal/ provincial co-operation in initiatives for the economic and socio-economic development of Nova Scotia in pursuit of certain broad objectives and in accordance with a strategy for development answered to the General Development Agreement. This strategy provides the framework within
May 14, 1976

which DREE operates. It is subject to review, of course, and does not preclude other joint or separate actions. Nevertheless, at this early stage of the implementation of the General Development Agreement, the bulk of DREE actions is directed toward implementing the strategy originally set forth.
The specific sectorial and geographic approaches mentioned in the GDA strategy include certain development aspects, as such, of the Halifax/Dartmouth metropolitan area; the development of the economic and social opportunities of the tourism-recreation and related sectors; and more generally, the funding of infrastructure required to support identified development opportunities.
Thus the General Development Agreement is an enabling agreement. Under it, individual sub-agreements are negotiated which will permit a comprehensive or package approach to the solution of specific development constraints or problems. However, isolated infrastructure projects are not undertaken simply for their own sake. They are supported only in pursuit of some broader development opportunity. Through negotiation with the provincial government, the federal government tried to develop an approach which will enhance the entire economic development of an area or a province. This is carried out through the signing of the special sub-agreements I referred to a moment ago.
Accordingly, as a matter of principle, the two specific actions covered by the motion would be considered by DREE only within the context of their relevance to a comprehensive development approach, whether sectorial or geographic. Thus far these projects have not been isolated, either by the provincial government or in DREE's own analytical work, as being sufficiently high priority to warrant immediate further attention. Now let us look specifically at the proposal in the hon. member's motion.
DREE, in co-operation with other federal agencies, including the Canadian government office of tourism, is now in the process of working with the province of Nova Scotia to develop a mechanism for federal/provincial cooperation in tourism.
Tourism is an important economic factor in the province. In 1974, for example, the estimated expenditure by visitors during the tourist season was approximately $76 million, yielding some $13.5 million in tax revenue.
The over-all goal of a tourism development program should be to improve the quality of life of Nova Scotia residents, not only economically but socially and environmentally as well. In this regard the tourist industry can add not only dollars to the economy but also make Nova Scotia a good place in which to work and live, which indeed it now is. Industrial and other development is enhanced by a healthy and agreeable environment which provides recreational possibilities for people. Such a situation is becoming increasingly important on this continent.
The nearness to a large population market, an abundance of historic attractions, the attractive resource base of the province compared to the deterioration of the environment elsewhere, add strength to Nova Scotia's ability to attract even greater numbers of visitors in the future.
Federal-Provincial Cost-Sharing
Much effort has gone into the promotional aspects of tourism, resulting in yearly increases of approximately 5 per cent in the numbers of tourists entering the province. More attention must be paid to the development aspect which can increase the economic impact through longer stays and highef dollars per day expenditures.
The non-economic aspects of tourism are difficult, if not impossible to measure quantitatively. Yet they cannot be ignored. There is evidence throughout the world, more particularly in Europe, the United Kingdom, and the United States, that concentration on the economics of tourism to the exclusion of other considerations can lead to environmental deterioration, with negative effects on the quality of life and a consequential backlash of public opinion. Nova Scotia is not immune from this danger, and already there have been public expressions of concern about it by individuals and groups.
Consequently in pursuing the developmental opportunities inherent in tourism, Nova Scotia's basic general aim is to exploit the economic potential of the industry to the fullest extent consistent with the preservation and ultimately the enhancement of a social, cultural, and physical environment that traditionally has been attractive to residents and visitors alike.
Considerable background work has already been done by the province. The provincial strategy provides for the concept of tourism travelways which are being established by utilized already-established trails, extending and rerouting some of them, and designating new ones. The Fundy Trail was originally proposed as a trail extending from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, to St. Stephen, New Brunswick.
In establishing a route for the proposed Fundy Vocation Trail, field investigations were conducted to determine the extent to which the location of existing highways was considered to be suitable and the locations where new construction would be required. Factors taken into consideration included the proximity of existing highways to the shoreline, scenery available along existing highways as compared with that available with relocation of the highway, and the extent to which the proposed trail would serve local traffic as well as tourist and other through traffic.
Based on the selected route and design standards, the estimated cost to establish the 887 mile-long Fundy Vacation Trail is as follows: Phase one, $37,700,000; Phase 2, $12 million; Phase 3, $16,800,000; Phase 4, $39,500,000; for a total of $106 million.
The Shubenacadie River crossing and completion of other links in the Fundy Trail in Nova Scotia are part of the Glooscap Trail. From the New Brunswick border the Glooscap Trail goes to Minudie and Joggins, and with the comletion of highways upgrading will proceed along the coast to Apple River, Parrsboro, Five Islands, and via the Shubenacadie River crossing will follow the Noel shore and terminate at Blomidon.
The provincial department of highways has work in progress on sections of highway between Apple River and Joggins and hope eventually to upgrade all sections of the Glooscap Trail. It has also started work on the substructure of the Shubenacadie River crossing. The total cost of this structure is estimated to be in the order of $7 million
