While it is quite possible the province may wish to pursue the possibility of DREE assistance toward these projects in the future, we have not been requested to share the cost of their construction.
Let me now turn to financing of a toll traffic tunnel under the Northwest Arm in Halifax. Under the special areas and highways legislation, consideration assistance was provided to the Halifax/Dartmouth area as a special area requiring special measures to facilitate economic expansion and social adjustment. Under this program financial assistance was made available to the metropolitan area, by way of grants and loans, for specific infrastructure projects such as roads, water and sewer systems, schools, etc. required to make this key centre more attractive as a site for future industrial and population growth. Much of this work was identified through the efforts of the metropolitan area planning committee whose task was to formulate a Halifax/Dartmouth regional development plan.
One of the objectives of this plan was "to create an effective regional transportation system, including an efficient highway system and the development of an effective transit system which will provide a viable alternative to the use of the private automobile". A task force under the metropolitan area planning committee was established to develop a total plan for urban transportation. Various possibilities were considered during the preparation of this plan. Initial studies projecting the current trend of population growth and development indicated excessive transportation costs by 1991. A third harbour crossing south of the existing two spans at an estimated cost of $100 million was a necessity. It was agreed, therefore, that a careful selection of the areas to be permitted to develop must be made. To this end, an urban form known as Scenario No. 14 was agreed upon.
The outstanding features of this scenario are that the expensive third harbour crossing is eliminated, the required size of the Northwest Arm crossing is eliminated, the required size of the Northwest Arm crossing was reduced to four lanes, and the necessity for an expressway through the central business district was removed. Road requirements increased slightly along the less expensive land routes such as the Bi-Centennial Highway. To achieve this urban form there must be a careful selection of the areas that are permitted to develop. The Bedford/Sackville and Cole Harbour areas are to be first priority residential, with the Burnside area of north Dartmouth between these two population centres to be commercial and industrial.
The south mainland Halifax area or Spryfield was second priority residential with in-fill only for the short term. The regional plan incorporating Scenario No. 14 was approved by the province in April, 1975. To facilitate traffic movement from this area to peninsula Halifax, the provincial department of highways is constructing Northwest Arm Drive between Spryfield and Bi-Centennial Drive. Completion of this highway, coupled with the

improvement under way at the Armdale rotary will improve traffic flows to peninsula Halifax and to other points via the new Dunbrack Street which is also under construction at the present time.
A general feasibility study of Halifax peninsula access carried out under the DREE special areas agreement in 1972 noted that the early construction of the Northwest Arm crossing introduces a high cost project which in the short term is then under-used and causes a significant and undesirable shift in route usage within the area of the isthmus. The "back-lag" or feeder route connections should be constructed first, with the Northwest Arm link scheduled for approximately 1981. Concurrent with the initial phase road construction would be extensive up-grading of the public transportation system with consideration being given to a "buses only" lane on the Arm crossing.
Various studies directly related to this Northwest Arm link have been carried out. One in the early 1960's made reference to a tunnel being a satisfactory solution to the physical impediment imposed by the Northwest Arm. No detailed investigation, to my knowledge, was pursued at that time, probably because of the obvious topographical constraints imposed by unfavourable land contours adjacent to the Arm. Since that time, with the construction of the Halifax Container Pier the feasibility of a tunnel is even more remote. The solution recommended in more recent studies of the problem suggests an aesthetically pleasing bridge structure as the most appropriate alternative. Costs of such a structure would be in the order of $15 million. In view of the recommendations of the approved regional plan, I am not aware that the province intends to proceed with any crossing over the Northwest Arm nor have I any reason to believe that it is a very high provincial priority for cost-sharing at this time.
The motion before us and its source surprise me somewhat, for two reasons, Mr. Speaker. We on this side of the House are constantly being lectured by the Tories for intruding into provincial jurisdictions. Yet they are constantly putting forward motions such as the one before us which would involve even greater intrusion into the provincial domain. Indeed it was only this morning that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was waxing indignantly, if not very knowledgeably, about that very topic.
Second, the opposition is constantly decrying the increase in federal spending. But its members have no hesitation in putting forward proposals to increase spending further. They would then be the first to condemn the government if it did just that.
Finally, while I can understand the hon. member's desire for such a development I personally cannot lend my support to this type of glamour project at a time when the basic transportation needs of the entire Atlantic area have yet to be fulfilled.

But I am going to talk about the Shubenacadie River crossing and in particular hopefully answer, in a most constructive, reasonable, logical way, two of the complaints raised by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne).
Before I get into the content of the resolution I would commend the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, who has been trying, not during this time of government restraint but ever since 1968 when he sat in this House as the member for Halifax-East Hants, by question and/or resolution, to get the federal government to move on something that, Mr. Speaker, has always been as perpetual as those tides that sweep in and sweep out of the Bay of Fundy.
Federal-Provincial Cost-Sharing
My riding takes in a good part of the Bay of Fundy, Mr. Speaker, and the tides that sweep in and sweep out with 55 foot crests are just about equal to the promises that have been made on the Shubenacadie River crossing by members in this House on the government side.
I agree with my hon. friend from Northumberland-Miramichi that obviously this is a joint federal-provincial matter. The premier of Nova Scotia, a former constituent of mine from the county of Hants, which would be so well helped and advanced by a Shubenacadie River crossing, more than two years ago promised that tenders would be called, and most likely tenders have been called this year.
We on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, know that whether we have times of restraint or whether we have times of expansion it takes a lot of hard, detailed, dogmatic, determined work by any member to try to focus the government's attention on something that seems to be so remote from this lovely capital of this lovely country. I agree Nova Scotia is miles away. For any of you who do not understand what is going on, just put out your left hand and extend your thumb, pretend your thumb is a sort of a joint to New Brunswick and that the curvature between the thumb and the forefinger is the Bay of Fundy. The Fundy Trail comes across the isthmus, the neck that joins Nova Scotia with New Brunswick, goes around the curve of the thumb and up the forefinger.
Because there is no Shubenacadie River crossing, for those of you here who are married, who were liberated many years ago and wear wedding rings, just project the path you now have to take. You cannot follow the Bay of Fundy-taking the inside of the angle of your thumb and forefinger-and see the beautiful scenery and go through some of the lovely villages along that shore without a Shubenacadie crossing at a certain point of the river. You have in effect to go up to your wedding ring where you have some fingers with little inlets. They do not run quite that way, but one of those inlets is the Shubenacadie River. Therefore you have to make such a diversion and take such a detour that the whole concept of the Fundy Trail is almost forgotten. You have to wend your way way inland, and then finally come back to the Bay of Fundy.
That is one of the reasons why this has been such a constructive, concrete proposal that has been advanced by my hon. friend. With all respect to my very fine colleague from Northumberland-Miramachi, the eminent parliamentary secretary of a department that needs much eminence, by the way, obviously this matter is in the provincial domain. An integrated effort is required by DREE and/or federal Public Works, along with the department in Nova Scotia.
The parliamentary secretary talks about spending restraints today. Separate and apart from the tourist potential that a Shubenacadie River crossing would give to western Nova Scotia-and my riding is western Nova Scotia-it would be of fundamental help to the economy of western Nova Scotia to get that crossing in place, so that traffic that comes from New Brunswick and central Canada into Nova Scotia does not have to take this wide detour almost across Nova Scotia and then double back to start servicing parts of western Nova Scotia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I welcome an opportunity this afternoon to participate in this particular discussion, first of all because of the nature of the hon. gentleman who moved the motion. I take his suggestions and his arguments very seriously. I think we always regard the comments that he makes and the motions he puts forward with seriousness, and we always examine the very worthy ideas that he presents to the House.
I am also pleased to have the benefit of the comments of the other members who have participated, the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) who has just taken his seat and who adds in a colourful way to the discussion, and my hon. friend from Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), who earlier in a very learned and detailed way put on the record certain of the aspects of this particular problem with which the federal government is concerned, particularly in relation to the work and terms

of reference of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
In all of the measures we have talked about this afternoon I think we can boil the discussion down to one of economics and developmental opportunities. The economy of Nova Scotia is generally a diversified one amongst its major sectors, and I think it is fair to say that some progress toward the reduction of disparity has been made in recent years. Of course we all know there is a great deal more to be done in the Atlantic region, in Nova Scotia and in other parts of the country, to continue working upon that challenge of economic disparity in Canada.
Measures indeed are under way, by this government and in conjunction with other governments, provincial and local across the country, to ensure continuous progress and indeed acceleration of improvements as they relate to economic opportunities in all parts of Canada, and toward the elimination so far as is possible in this land of the economic disparities which exist between regions. The measures, and I think it is useful to bear them in mind in any discussion of this kind, include encouraging the expansion or maintenance of viable long-term employment opportunities and optimum quality of life, within Nova Scotia in this particular case, increasing the earned incomes of the people of the province, and assisting in development of a dynamic and creative provincial economy which will encourage the growth and stability of economic activity in the province.
I know that the hon. gentleman who moved the motion this afternoon who is from Annapolis Valley, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence, the former Nova Scotian from Winnipeg North Centre, and others share those general objectives, so I hope hon. members will not take what is said perhaps specifically in terms of opposition to any individual idea as opposition to any of the general principles that are involved, because certainly that general opposition is not intended.
I think the specific measures to which I have referred briefly could be described as broad, general objectives which have the co-operation of the federal, provincial and municipal governments jointly pursuing a consistent and co-ordinated course of action involving specific sectoral and geographic approaches. This I think was the gist of the argument that was presented to the House earlier today by my friend from Northumberland-Miramichi, that is, the need to approach the developmental challenges in any particular region of the country in a co-ordinated, consistent and co-operative way so that the actions of one level of government or the projects of one particular area of government do not act in competition to or in conflict with the work being undertaken by another area of government.
The areas of developmental opportunity really are numerous. I think I would like to take a moment of the time of the House to highlight them. I think of the development of new or expanded employment opportunities throughout the province by the identification and implementation of appropriate developmental opportunities; the design and implementation of urban and rural developmental measures required to support and really
May 14, 1976

promote economic and socio-economic opportunities as they are found to exist; the development in the Atlantic region of the resource industries of fishing obviously, agriculture, forestry, and mining through measures to improve their efficiency, productivity and optimim resource utilization, including intensified research and the further processing of their primary products. Then there is the development, specifically as my friend from North-umberland-Miramichi said, of the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area with special emphasis on high technology industries, communication, distribution, and transportation related industries, and a wide range of business and personnel services consistent with its evolution as a major business and service centre.
Next we have the continued growth of the primary and secondary processing of imported and domestic raw and semi-finished materials in the Strait of Canso area, including such industries that may be associated with or in any way dependent upon its existing base of petroleum refining and related services and secondary industries. We have the fostering of economic and social opportunities associated with tourism and recreation and other related sectors. This is a very relevant factor in connection with at least the Fundy Trail part of the proposal in the motion today. There is a provision of special interim assistance required to eliminate impediments which might threaten the retention and maintenance of otherwise viable opportunities and industries. Further, Mr. Speaker, there is the development of spin-off opportunities related to the supply, service, exploration, extraction, and distribution of off-shore oil and gas.
What I have tried to provide to the House is a partial list. The list could go on, but I have provided at least a partial list of some of the fundamental concerns and developmental opportunities in the Atlantic region, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, which present to a provincial government, to municipalities, and to the Government of Canada a range of opportunities for action.
Of course the challenge or really the dilemma before any government, either at the provincial level or at the senior level, is really sorting out among all those authorities what really can be acted upon in an urgent sort of way, what has priority attention, and really what must be left in terms of priority for a later time and for further consideration. At the present moment in time I believe it is fair to say that both in the assessment of the provincial administration and in the view of the various involved agencies of the Government of Canada, a number of other areas of challenge and opportunity really must at this stage have a higher priority than the two specific programs which are mentioned in the motion before us this afternoon.
As you will know, Mr. Speaker, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has signed three subsidiary
Federal-Provincial Cost-Sharing agreements with the province of Nova Scotia under the provisions of the General Development Agreement which generally covers the province. Taken together they call for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to spend a total of $104 million on developmental schemes. For the information of the House, Mr. Speaker, these agreements include the metropolitan Halifax-Dartmouth area developmental agreement, the Strait of Canso area development agreement, and the Canada-Nova Scotia subsidiary agreement on mineral development.
I could take some considerable time to run through the various aspects of these programs which are extremely important because they demonstrate a concern at both the federal and provincial level for the developmental and economic challenges and opportunities that are present in the Atlantic area. I think it would be useful for the House to have that detailed kind of explanation on the record because it is an encouraging one, one which looks toward the future and really holds out some substantial optimism and encouragement for the developmental prospects of the Atlantic region, particularly the province of Nova Scotia. Unfortunately time does not permit.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to devote a brief word or two to the question of transportation per se, I suppose most particularly on the Fundy Trail aspect of the motion before us. We of course have not had in the past a generally co-ordinated suggestion, argument or proposal from the Atlantic provinces about a general program of highway or road improvement as we have had for example, in the case of some of the western provinces. Indeed in the west we have a comprehensive strengthening program for highways in the western provinces. Recently of course we have had the benefit of some views presented by the four Atlantic ministers of transportation or highways as they presented to the Government of Canada a detailed report, which report presently is under study by officials of the Ministry of Transport.
I hope the analysis of that report will lead to some constructive and positive conclusions which will be of benefit to the province of Nova Scotia, particularly the area which the hon. member has so dedicatedly worked for over the past many years in connection with the proposal now before the House.
